analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture, import, and use of all forms of asbestos in the United States.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first committee: after being referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Environment Subcommittee in early 2018, it received no markup, no vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA to identify every way asbestos enters and moves through the U.S. economy, then impose rules that permanently eliminate the chance of people or the environment being exposed to it. Asbestos is a mineral fiber that causes mesothelioma, lung cancer, and other fatal diseases decades after exposure; the United States never fully banned it, and it was still being imported when this bill was introduced. The bill set firm deadlines — an assessment within 90 days, an elimination rule within 18 months, with a narrow presidential exemption for national-security uses that have no reasonable alternative.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who might otherwise be exposed to asbestos in the future — workers in plants that process it, people in buildings and homes containing it, and communities near disposal sites. Since asbestos diseases often take decades to appear, the main beneficiaries are future generations, plus the families of the roughly 40,000 Americans who die each year from asbestos-related diseases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, families, and future generations exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA, within 90 days of enactment, to identify and assess the current and anticipated importation, distribution, uses of, and exposures to asbestos [S2][S3].

Requires the EPA within 18 months to issue a rule imposing prohibitions and restrictions — including on manufacture, processing, use, distribution in commerce, and disposal — chosen to 'permanently eliminate the possibility of exposure to asbestos' [S3].

Beginning one year after the rule takes effect, no person could manufacture, process, use, distribute, or dispose of any form of asbestos or asbestos-containing products except as allowed by the rule, with deadlines for each prohibition set as soon as practicable and no later than one year after the rule [S3].

Provides only a narrow exemption: the President could exempt a use for up to three years only if it were necessary for national security, no reasonable alternative existed, and the use posed no unreasonable health or environmental risk, judged without weighing costs [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that import, manufacture, or sell asbestos and asbestos-containing products would have to find substitutes or exit those lines of business. Since 2016, the main continuing U.S. use of raw asbestos has been by chlor-alkali plants that make chlorine using asbestos-based technology — a general-knowledge explanation of who the ban would hit, not something the bill text itself names. Replacement technologies and substitutes exist but cost money.

drawbacks.text: National-security exemption could be renewed indefinitely: the President could grant a new three-year exemption repeatedly by making a fresh determination each time, so a determined administration could keep a use alive for decades [S3].

The one-year phase-out starting a year after the rule is faster than some remediation timelines, and critics of asbestos bans generally argue that removal and replacement of asbestos-containing materials can itself disturb fibers and raise exposure, and that regulated uses (such as in chlorine production) have alternatives only at a cost — a cost argument the bill text forecloses by requiring the risk finding to be made 'without consideration of costs or other nonrisk factors' [S3].

The bill directs the EPA to 'permanently eliminate the possibility' of exposure — a zero-exposure standard that is technically difficult for legacy asbestos already in buildings and the environment, and the bill does not fund removal of existing asbestos, so the most common exposure pathway for the public would remain largely unaddressed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — cutting off new asbestos imports and uses that cause fatal cancers decades later — is large and cheap relative to its cost, because the number of continuing U.S. uses is small and substitutes exist for nearly all of them. The bill's real weakness is that it targets ongoing commerce while doing little about the asbestos already in millions of buildings, which is where most Americans' exposure risk lies. The renewability of the national-security exemption is a modest loophole. Overall, a well-designed bill with a narrower scope than its name suggests.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Environment Subcommittee from March 2018 until the Congress ended, and no one ever brought it to a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 27, 2018, by Rep. Suzanne Bonamici with 8 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and three days later to the Subcommittee on Environment, where its consideration ended [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without the committee reporting the bill or the House voting on it [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies still importing and using asbestos in 2018 kept doing so, since the status quo — an incomplete ban under which asbestos could still legally enter the country — continued for at least another Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies still importing and using asbestos

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and named it for Alan Reinstein, an asbestos-disease activist

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill during the 115th Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on; with the House Republican majority controlling the committee calendar, the bill got no vote [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have prohibited importation, manufacture, processing, use, and disposal of asbestos within roughly two years, ending their continuing business lines. Asbestos exposure causes fatal cancers decades later, so their revenue comes at the public's long-term health expense.

industries.industry: Chlor-alkali chemical plants (chlorine producers using asbestos technology)
industries.note: These plants were the main continuing U.S. users of raw asbestos, using it in technology that produces chlorine for water treatment; the ban would force a switch to membrane-based technology that avoids asbestos. Chlorine itself is a public good, so the industry's loss cuts both ways.

industries.industry: Substitute and remediation industries (asbestos abatement, replacement materials)
industries.note: A ban would create demand for asbestos-free substitutes and for safely removing existing asbestos materials, expanding markets for abatement and replacement products that protect the public.
